item.title: China-EU trade talks rebalance, stabilize relations
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
China-EU trade talks rebalance, stabilize relations Partners key to each other will address concerns, frictions in WTO framework The second round of China-EU trade and investment consultations concluded in Beijing last week with a series of understandings and deliverables, offering a counterweight to growing global protectionist pressures, and underscoring both sides' continued engagement to stabilize and balance one of the world's most vital bilateral economic relationships. After two days of intensive talks co-chaired by Minister of Commerce Wang Wentao and European Commissioner for Trade and Economic Security Maros Sefcovic, the two sides have agreed to maintain stable bilateral economic and trade ties and make them more balanced. Their joint statement set out 16 specific points of consensus covering trade and investment balance, export controls, intellectual property rights, and World Trade Organization, or WTO, reform. According to the readout, both sides will continue, within the framework of WTO rules, to explore the possibility of tariff reductions on certain goods. An understanding has been reached on trade in hybrid vehicles in a WTO-compliant manner. The two sides, which traded $828.1 billion of goods in 2025, also discussed in depth ways to address each other's concerns on equal footing, expand two-way market access, and promote a dynamic balance in China-EU trade, covering topics including medical devices, cosmetics, pharmaceuticals, inverters, and agri-food products. To help increase imports of medical devices from the EU, a matchmaking event will be held during the 9th China International Import Expo, which will take place in Shanghai in November. Despite some doom-and-gloom headlines that preceded the talks, the consultations ended without acrimony and produced a 16-point joint statement that spoke for itself, said Wolfgang Roehr, a former German consul general in Shanghai, who is currently a visiting scholar at the Center for Cultural Studies on Science and Technology in China at the Technical University of Berlin. "It shows that Brussels and Beijing, if push comes to shove, can overcome differences — even if these are severe — and find a practical compromise," he said. "This inspires hope that both sides can, at present and in the future, agree also on further issues on trade, and indeed, on questions in other areas." Business responded positively to the Beijing talks, with "relief" the predominant sentiment, said Michael Schumann, chairman of the board at Germany's Federal Association for Economic Development and Foreign Trade. "What companies need above all is predictability," he said. "Every new headline about a possible trade war delays investment decisions and puts supply chains under additional strain. A negotiated understanding, a clear timetable for further talks, and above all the commitment to keep talking are therefore precisely the signals businesses have been waiting for." The Ministry of Commerce said China and the EU will hold the third meeting of the consultation mechanism in March, with a ministerial video meeting scheduled for January to maintain communication ahead of the next round of talks. Qu Hongbin, former chief China economist at HSBC, said jaw-jaw is always better — and cheaper — than war-war, given that the economies of China and the EU are "overwhelmingly complementary". "Trying to forcefully decouple two economies of this scale is like trying to unbake a cake — messy, expensive, and ultimately unproductive," he said. The benefits of choosing pragmatism over mutually assured destruction would extend well beyond China and the EU, Qu said. "It is a shot in the arm for global stability. At a time when the global economy is struggling with fragmented supply chains and sticky inflation, a stable EU-China economic relationship is a massive stabilizer. Lower uncertainty means lower capital risk premiums, something global markets desperately need right now," he said.

item.title: Expert urges stronger climate adaptation
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
Expert urges stronger climate adaptation Report calls for locally tailored upgrade of infrastructure and lifeline systems A leading Chinese urban planning expert has called on the government to strengthen its adaptive capacity in the face of escalating climate-related disasters, highlighting transformative capacity and coping capacity as the most urgent priorities among core capacities. Li Xiaojiang, a national engineering survey and design master and former president of the China Academy of Urban Planning and Design, made the remarks following a study presented at the annual general meeting of the China Council for International Cooperation on Environment and Development, a high-level international advisory body for the Chinese government, held on Sept 27-29 in Beijing. Li serves as the Chinese co-team lead of the CCICED scoping study on building a climate-adaptive society, which developed an assessment framework based on five core capacities for climate resilience: preventive, coping, recovery, transformative and long-term adaptive. The CCICED study comes as China pursues the goal of basically establishing a climate-adaptive society by 2035. It notes that climate adaptation has become a pillar of national security, sustainable development and public well-being, and recommends making it a mainstream consideration in planning, infrastructure, finance, technology and public governance. According to the study, coping capacity is defined as the ability to reduce disaster losses following extreme weather events. Transformative capacity refers to the ability of current social, economic and governance systems to proactively transform themselves into new systems with different characteristics when facing expected disaster risks. Li, a special adviser to CCICED, stressed that climate adaptation is fundamentally different from climate mitigation. While cutting emissions produces global benefits that are relatively easy to measure, adaptation responds to localized hazards whose types, timing, exposure and losses vary sharply across regions. "There is no universal template for adaptation," Li said. "There can only be lessons that are transferable among regions facing similar types of risks." For instance, a coastal city may face sea-level rise, storm surges and typhoons, whereas cities in central or northern China are more exposed to extreme rainfall and flooding. Meanwhile, the Chengdu-Chongqing region faces extreme heat, drought and mounting pressure on energy and water systems, he explained. The CCICED study's case studies examine Shanghai's exposure to sea-level rise, Shenzhen's challenges as a high-density city facing extreme rainfall, the Chengdu-Chongqing region's vulnerability to extreme heat, and the changing risks in arid northern China as some areas experience warming and wetting. Because of these regional differences, Li emphasized that local assessments are essential. Each region should evaluate its specific climate hazards, infrastructure weaknesses, and adaptive capacity, and then identify the most urgent actions. The study recommends linking climate adaptation capacity assessments with differentiated local strategies. Li pointed out that "transformative capacity" represents one of China's most important long-term gaps. Beyond repairing damage, transformation requires changing land-use decisions, construction methods and patterns of production and daily life. In extreme cases, the right choice may be to avoid areas facing unacceptable risks rather than repeatedly rebuilding in harm's way, Li said. He cited the reconstruction of Beichuan county in a different location after the devastating 2008 Wenchuan earthquake in Sichuan province as an example. "Relocation-based reconstruction should not be undertaken lightly, as it carries enormous costs and far-reaching social implications," Li stressed. "But that, in itself, is a form of transformation. It means not putting people and development back into danger, but proactively changing our approach so that long-term adaptive capacity can be built." He also emphasized the critical importance of lifeline infrastructure, including power, transport, drainage and emergency systems. Losses during extreme weather events often stem not only from the primary disaster, but from cascading failures such as outages, blocked transport and damage to underground facilities. The report calls for locally tailored upgrading and retrofitting of infrastructure and lifeline systems, including flood control facilities, energy and communications infrastructure, urban municipal facilities, transport systems, rural production areas and critical underground spaces. It also recommends revising engineering standards for climate resilience. Li urged policymakers to make full use of the new round of infrastructure investment to raise the quality and disaster resilience of China's built environment. He summarized existing weaknesses as low coverage, low standards in older systems, uneven construction quality and inadequate maintenance. Although adaptation projects may not always generate strong direct financial returns, Li noted that their national economic benefits are substantial because they prevent damage to lives, property, supply chains and broader economic activity.

item.title: 3 children, 1 adult killed in US school shooting: media
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
3 children, 1 adult killed in US Oregon elementary school shooting: media SAN FRANCISCO -- At least three children and one adult were killed Thursday in a shooting at Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, US state of Oregon, CBS News reported, citing law enforcement sources. Bend police spokesperson Sheila Miller said at a news briefing that police received a report at about 12:59 pm local time of a person firing shots into a vehicle outside the school. Within about a minute, multiple 911 calls reported that the gunman had entered the school and begun shooting. Police officers arrived at the scene and found the suspect shot inside the school. Authorities have not confirmed who fired the fatal shot. The suspect was shot and killed by a bystander, law enforcement sources said. Earlier, the police spokesperson said two people were transported to a local hospital with their conditions unknown. The total number of victims was not clear, Miller said.

item.title: Old department stores sell nostalgic journey to past
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-16
When Qiao Yanxiong was a boy in the 1950s and '60s, the neighborhood around Yong'an Road in Beijing was quiet and leafy. Neighbors all knew one another, and familiar local businesses catered to the daily needs of the community. The streets were lined with small shops and outlets — a laundry, a grain store, a bank and a bookstore. However, one emporium, the Yong'an Road Department Store, was the heartbeat of daily life. Qiao, 71, who now runs the department store, grew up nearby. As a boy, he shopped there with his parents for virtually everything. Nearly seven decades after the store opened on Jan 1,1958, he has one final goal. "I plan to work until 2028, finish the 70th anniversary celebration and then retire," he said proudly. Qiao remembers the department store as a place where shoppers could find almost everything they needed, from underwear and socks to pots and pans, bicycles and household appliances. The neighborhood and its surroundings have changed dramatically since those years. Many longtime residents have moved away, while supermarkets and online shopping have transformed the way people buy goods. The store's floor space has also shrunk. Its two main sales areas now occupy about 200 square meters, and its inventory no longer includes fabrics, bicycles and household appliances. But its identity remains deliberately old-fashioned, Qiao said. "Old store, old merchants, old products, old brands, old ways of selling and old ways of settling payments," he said. "The key word is 'old.'" In the past, one of its busiest sections was the fabric counter, a small space where bolts of cloth were stacked beneath clothing and quilt covers. A sewing machine sat behind the counter, and sales staff doubled as seamsters, sewing items for customers when business was slow. In the late 1970s and early 1980s, customers queued all day to buy fabric, particularly toward the end of the year when fabric coupons were about to expire. Even plain white cloth often sold out. The counter remained busy until the 1990s when ready-made clothes became cheaper with a wider variety.

item.title: Scholars look to future of archaeology
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
Scholars look to future of archaeology Congress: Research provides solid insights Drawing on a century of archaeological experience in China, lessons learned from past excavations should illuminate the future, guiding the discipline forward with renewed purpose, scholars said at the 5th Congress of Chinese Archaeology, which opened on Thursday in Yuncheng, Shanxi province. The theme for this year's three-day event, one of the highest-level academic forums for archaeological studies in China, is "The history and future of archaeology". Chen Xingcan, chairman of the Society for Chinese Archaeology, said the theme of this year's congress calls for looking back on history, paying tribute to elder generations of archaeologists, consolidating the disciplinary foundation rooted in present-day practice, and charting a new chapter for archaeology going forward. The choice of Yuncheng as the venue for this grand event is itself a tribute to the starting point of a century of Chinese archaeology. Exactly 100 years ago, in October 1926, archaeologist Li Ji (1896-1979), who is regarded as the father of Chinese archaeology, broke ground with his spade at the Xiyin site in Xiaxian county, Yuncheng. The Neolithic site dates from 5,200 to 6,000 years ago. That single spadeful of earth opened a new chapter in history — the first modern scientific archaeological excavation independently led by a Chinese scholar. Together with several other sites where archaeological efforts began in the 1920s, the Xiyin site has been recognized as part of the beginning of modern Chinese archaeology. In May 2023, President Xi Jinping visited the Yuncheng Museum and called for further efforts to advance the national research project on tracing the origins of Chinese civilization and the historical research on this civilization, and to improve the capabilities of protecting and utilizing cultural relics and passing on Chinese cultural heritage. Chen, the archaeology society chairman, said, "Today, we converge in Yuncheng to hold the congress, as a concrete endeavor of turning the spirit of President Xi's important instructions into academic practice." Zheng Yuan, deputy director of the Shanxi Provincial Institute of Cultural Relics and Archaeology, said in her keynote speech that from 1926 to 2026, the century-long research journey of the Xiyin site has been just like a mirror, clearly reflecting the development of China's archaeology. "The year 1926 marked the starting point of self-directed research by Chinese scholars, which focused on collecting artifacts and understanding the stratigraphic layers (the soil, sediment and rock that have built up over time at an archaeological site) and dating of the site," Zheng said. "The year 1994 saw renewed study after China's archaeological system had matured, with a focus on understanding the local cultural sequence," Zheng said. "The latest excavation, conducted from last year to this year, represents a new exploration in an era that emphasizes science-based archaeology and the tracing of Chinese civilization's origins," she said. "By gathering information on the settlement, subsistence and social structure of Xiyin society, we have deepened our understanding of the origins of Chinese civilization," she added. Zheng noted that the site has witnessed the development of China's archaeology, from introducing Western methodologies to establishing an indigenous disciplinary system, then moving toward multidisciplinary research, and now toward a public cultural undertaking to serve the public's spiritual needs. "The past century of research on the Xiyin site is the epitome of the growth of China's archaeology, and is about generations of scholars who have continued to study the same site. From interpreting objects to reconstructing society, and from reading stratigraphic layers to comprehending civilization, such sustained research sheds light on Chinese civilization with solid evidence," she said. Shi Jinsong, director of the Chinese Academy of Social Sciences' Institute of Archaeology, said the century-long journey of Chinese archaeology offers an opportunity to reflect on the future of the discipline and even human society. "We can see from our experience that archaeology contributes to civilizational studies mainly through two approaches: tracing the origins of Chinese civilization and promoting mutual learning among civilizations," he said. Looking inward, archaeologists trace the origins, development paths and distinctive features of Chinese civilization, giving it a clearer presence among world civilizations. Looking outward, in-depth and broad comparative studies with other countries and civilizations reveal the similarities and differences between civilizations, providing a richer and more comprehensive understanding of global civilizations. "Both point to the same goals — to understand the lineage of civilizational development from ancient remains and to unveil the details of historical progress and the drivers of civilizational development. On that basis, we can reflect on the development direction of human society," Shi said. The congress this year includes 28 professional committees, which will together give more than 570 reports in 28 parallel sessions focusing on different historical periods and different fields of archaeological studies, such as underwater archaeology, zooarchaeology, which is the study of animal remains from archaeological sites, and archaeometry, the use of scientific techniques in dating archaeological remains. Beyond the academic sessions, the congress will also reach out to the public. As part of the event, 22 public lectures are being organized in Yuncheng and other cities of Shanxi.

item.title: From bouldering to BMX, emerging sports gain a grip
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
From bouldering to BMX, emerging sports gain a grip China's recent success in exciting new disciplines inspires a new generation As the National Day holiday drew to a close, young people took turns tackling a rock climbing wall at a gym in Xi'an, Shaanxi province. Some carefully tested each hold before moving upward, while others dropped back onto the mats and prepared to try again. For Zhao Yu'an, a young climber at the gym, the appeal lay in the challenge itself — figuring out how to complete a route and sharing the experience with friends. Earlier in the holiday, thousands of kilometers away, Chinese climbers had faced a very different test at the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games. Zhang Yuetong won the women's bouldering gold medal, while Chu Shouhong claimed the men's speed climbing title with a time of 4.71 seconds. From street culture, climbing communities and grassroots training spaces to the Asian Games and Olympics, emerging sports such as skateboarding, sport climbing and breaking are reaching wider audiences in China. Major competitions have brought these disciplines greater visibility and helped establish clearer pathways for elite athletes. Their performances, in turn, inspire more young people to take up the sports.

item.title: Guizhou village carries Long March spirit into new era
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
Xinghong village in Guizhou carries Long March spirit into new era More than 90 years after the Red Army's four crossings of the Chishui River, Xinghong village, located on the river's banks, is writing a new chapter for a new era of the Long March story. From the Red Army's unwavering commitment to serving the people to the village's current efforts to pursue change, Xinghong has carried forward the spirit of perseverance. Dai Xiaoyong, Party secretary of the village administered by the city of Chishui, Guizhou province, gave up a high-paying job as a doctor to return to his hometown. He has led villagers in developing under-forest black-bone chicken farming and livestream e-commerce, while putting idle resources to productive use. Dai said these initiatives have led to more opportunities for the local residents. "When it comes to the people, no issue is too small. Doing every small thing well is how you accomplish something big," Dai said.

item.title: New China-DPRK border bridge opens to traffic
item.description:
Published: 2026-10-15
New China-DPRK border bridge over Yalu River opens to traffic SHENYANG -- The new China-DPRK Yalu River bridge officially opened to traffic on Thursday, with both sides jointly holding an opening ceremony on this cross-border artery. The cable-stayed bridge over the Yalu River serves as a cross-border transport link between the city of Dandong in Northeast China's Liaoning province and the city of Sinuiju in North Pyongan province in the Democratic People's Republic of Korea (DPRK). The double-pylon and double-cable-plane bridge features a 28.5-meter-wide deck designed with four lanes for two-way traffic, while its water navigation clearance is designed for vessels of up to the 3,000-ton class. The new bridge will further facilitate trade and people-to-people exchanges between the two countries, Chinese foreign ministry spokeswoman Mao Ning said on Wednesday. China and the DPRK are friendly neighbors connected by mountains and rivers, and the new bridge is an important facility for connectivity between the two countries, Mao noted at a regular press briefing. Dandong boasts China's largest border trade port with the DPRK. Before the new road bridge, the Yalu River Bridge, also known as the China-DPRK Friendship Bridge, served as a combined road-rail bridge. The old one, however, could only accommodate trucks weighing no more than 20 tons for one-way road traffic. China and the DPRK in 2010 agreed to build a new road bridge downstream from the old one.
